segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's last doha: the musk is in the deer, and Ram is in every heart. Where did you stop hunting and find it already near? Day nine hundred twenty-four.

It's night, and the river is high from the rains. A young man has come home to find his wife gone to her parents' house across the water, and he can't stand to wait until morning. So he crosses the swollen river, in the dark, and climbs up to her window. She is not charmed. She's embarrassed, and she tells him so, sharply. If you loved Ram, she says, the way you love this body of flesh and bone, you'd be free. The young man goes away and doesn't come back. That's how tradition tells the turning of Tulsidas.
screen: `A SWOLLEN RIVER AT NIGHT.` → `HIS WIFE'S SHARP WORDS.` → `HE TURNS TO RAM.`

segments.voice: Tulsidas became a poet of Ram, and his great work is the Ramcharitmanas, the story of Ram retold in Awadhi, a language people spoke, not the Sanskrit of the older Ramayana. For the next three days we'll stay with him, starting at the poem's front door. The Manas opens with a short run of Sanskrit verses, as if Tulsidas bows at the threshold in the old language before stepping inside in the new one. The very first verse bows to Vani, the goddess of speech, and to Vinayaka, Ganesha: makers of letters and meanings, of the flavors and meters of verse, and of everything auspicious. A poet, before writing a word, thanks the one who gives words, and the one who clears the road. Then comes a line that's easy to miss. Tulsidas says why he is writing: for the happiness of his own heart, svantah sukhaya. Not for fame. He tells the story of Ram because telling it makes him glad. And the poem explains its own name. It says Shiva composed this story first and kept it in his own mind, his manas, and so it's called the Manas of Ram's deeds. Tulsidas, in other words, says he's passing on something Shiva has been holding in his heart. Now look back at this week. Namdev and a dog and a turning temple. Tukaram's split sugarcane, and his notebooks rising from the river. Kabir's three dohas, each turning the hunt back on the hunter. And Tulsidas, turned around by his wife's sharp words, sitting down to write for the joy of it.
screen: `THE MANAS, IN AWADHI.` · `A BOW TO VANI AND VINAYAKA.` · `FOR MY OWN HEART'S JOY.` · then, large: `KEPT IN SHIVA'S MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of one thing you do, or used to do, simply because it makes you glad: singing in the car, drawing, cooking, telling a story to a child. Not for anyone's praise, not to prove anything. Let it come back to you with its sound and its feel. Notice what happens inside you when you remember it. Then, the way Tulsidas bowed before he started, let yourself be thankful for whatever gave you that gift. If you pray, you can offer that thanks to God. The bell holds the time.
Tulsidas. The poet of the Ramcharitmanas, who bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at its door, and wrote the story of Ram for the happiness of his own heart.
Your line: for my own heart's joy. Today, do one small thing for the joy of it, svantah sukhaya. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Hindus who love Ram read and sing the Ramcharitmanas at home and in temples, sometimes all the way through over several days, and its verses are chanted and staged in Ram Lila performances.

fork.setup: you've crossed a flooded river at night to see your wife, and she tells you to love Ram as much as you love her body. what does Tulsidas do?
options: argue that he did it out of love.
go away and turn his life toward Ram.
wait at her parents' house until she relents.
fork.reveal: tradition says he left and turned to Ram, and in time wrote the Ramcharitmanas.

original.note: Awadhi title, in Devanagari: the Manas of Ram's deeds, a name the poem ties to Shiva's mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old retelling of the Ramayana.
what it means: a poet bows at the door, then tells Ram's story in the people's language for the joy of his own heart.
what a scholar hears: the poem says Shiva composed the story and kept it in his manas, and takes its name from that.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the opening shloka (varnanam arthasanghanam... vande vani vinayakau) is fairly summarized, and that svantah sukhaya comes from the seventh opening shloka.
Confirm the naming passage in Bal Kand (Shiva composed it, kept it in his manas, and named it Ramcharitmanas).
The wife's rebuke is hagiography, framed as tradition; her name (Ratnavali) is not spoken. Confirm the paraphrase of her words.
Day 924 is a week end: look-back names days 918-923 (written by this agent) and today.
'Not the Sanskrit of the older Ramayana' assumes Valmiki's Ramayana as the older work; confirm wording.
Original: रामचरितमानस, stress guide raam-cha-rit-MAA-nas; confirm.
howItsDone mentions full recitations and Ram Lila; confirm phrasing.

Audit pass: the rebuke said 'half as much'; the doha usually attributed to Ratnavali (asthi charm maya deh mama...) says such love, not half, so it now reads 'the way you love this body'. The first shloka's rasas and chhandas were compressed to 'the music of verse'; now 'the flavors and meters of verse'. Cut 'not to win an argument with the scholars', which the opening does not say.
